The third installment of Er Mu’s translation of Trevor Cox’s Now You’re Talking. Work is getting busier, the editors admit, but they like the book so much that they hope to finish translating it even if original posts stop. Earlier installments: the introduction and evolution, part 1.

The chapter traces the mammalian middle ear. At the threshold of hearing the eardrum moves by about the diameter of a hydrogen atom, and the ossicles act as an amplifier: because the eardrum is so much larger than the stapes that passes sound on to the inner ear, the signal is boosted about 17-fold, roughly 30 dB. Their history is a case of exaptation. In 1837 the German anatomist Karl Bogislaus Reichert saw in pig embryos that the malleus and incus begin as cartilage behind the jaw, yet he never accepted Darwin’s theory, to Ernst Haeckel’s scorn. Evolutionary biologist Vera Weisbecker of the University of Queensland explains why development preserves such ancestral traces.

Over some 80 million years, as synapsids became mammals, two jaw bones shrank and moved to the ear; Yanoconodon allini, a 10-centimeter mammal from 125 million years ago found in the Yanshan region of China, preserves an intermediate stage. Since fossil ossicles are scarce, Weisbecker’s team CT-scanned young marsupials, whose ossicles still start out on the jaw. The bones detached before they shrank, which suggests that feeding, perhaps the arrival of molars to crush hard seeds, drove the separation, and hearing high-frequency airborne sound came afterward.

Translated into Chinese by Er Mu (edited by Er Mu and Fanyu Meng) from Trevor Cox’s Now You’re Talking: Human Conversation from the Neanderthals to Artificial Intelligence (2018). About the book.
